moves.spoken: The Scotch is one of the oldest openings there is — the whole idea is to contest the centre at once and open lines for the bishop. It's principled, but it comes with a catch.

The downside is that the knight has moved twice already — and that's dangerous, because it lets the other side develop pieces while attacking them at the same time. That's developing with tempo, and the bishop to c5 does exactly that.
Rather than recapture, bring the queen to f6 — and crucially don't grab the knight. It's an in-between move, and the knight isn't going anywhere while the opponent scrambles to defend.

That f-pawn defence weakens the king. Recapture with the d-pawn, because it opens the diagonal for the bishop — a reminder that when choosing between recaptures, pick the one that also serves your development.

Develop the knight — and notice the opponent simply can't castle. That's why the f-pawn move is so reviled: it opened the diagonal, and with the bishop already glaring down it, tucking the king to safety becomes a nightmare.

The bishop move blunders a piece, and it teaches the single biggest beginner affliction — tunnel vision. The opponent saw only that they were attacking a pawn and never noticed the queen eyeing the bishop. Most mistakes at the improving level are exactly this narrowing of view.
Now the theme of the whole game — converting a material advantage. Being up material is only half the job; turning it into a win with clean, purposeful play is the skill worth drilling.

A pawn just advanced — so run the check: whenever a pawn moves it leaves weaknesses in its wake. Two pawns are now loose, and when you see a good capture, look for a better one: taking on b2 not only grabs the pawn but also hits the rook in the corner, which can't escape.

And a pattern to file away: if the opponent tries to x-ray-defend the rook, the queen and king end up on the same diagonal — so always look for a pin whenever the queen and king line up like that. It happens astonishingly often.
The rook is simply collected — now up a rook and a piece, hitting the knight, and the opponent still can't castle. That inability to get the king safe is what ultimately sinks them.

Before pressing on, evacuate the queen so it doesn't get stranded in the corner — retreating it to e5, where it also pins a pawn against the king. Rescue the far-flung piece before it becomes a liability.

For the record, the correct defence was the queen to f3, and the trade that follows leads to an endgame that's appeared thousands of times at the top level. The queen sortie was tempting — developing and eyeing a scholar's-mate threat — but the calm defensive move was the right one.
